fields.meta_title: Brand Perception Survey Questions and Template | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Brand perception survey questions, a template, and four studies: a rival tracker, a pack test, first-word themes, and an employer brand check.
fields.h1: Build a Brand Perception Survey You Can Track Over Time
fields.hero_description: Build a brand perception survey that rates you against rivals each quarter and keeps every answer in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: The Parts That Make Perception Data Comparable
fields.features_subheading: Each piece keeps one wave's numbers readable next to the last.
fields.feature_1:
Attribute statements on one fixed scale

Rate the brand on four to six statements, such as "Fees are fair" or "Easy to reach a person," each on a 1 to 5 scale. Locked wording keeps every wave in line with the last.
fields.feature_2:
Competitors rated on the same statements

Ask the same statements about two or three competitors, shown in random order. Your score then reads against the market, and a rival the respondent has never heard of is skipped.
fields.feature_3:
An open first-word question before any list

Ask for one word about the brand before any name or logo appears on screen. Theme rules you write group near-synonyms, such as cheap and affordable, and count each theme weekly.
fields.feature_4:
Scores split by customer and non-customer

A screening question records whether each person bought from you this year. Every chart filters on it, plus region and age band, and segments under 50 answers are marked thin.
fields.feature_5:
A message when an attribute slips

Set the drop that matters, such as half a point between waves. The brand lead then gets a Slack message or email naming the statement, both scores, and how the rivals moved.
fields.feature_6:
Answers you keep, code you can export

Responses land in a database you own, one row per respondent per wave. Export the whole survey app to your GitHub repository on paid plans, then keep changing it with a prompt.
fields.why_title: Why Build Your Perception Survey With Emergent?
fields.why_description: Theme rules and alert thresholds are code you can read. Change them with a prompt, and keep adding waves with no cap on responses.

fields.tab_content_1:
Four statements, two rivals, one quarterly score

Each quarter, 400 adults in a regional bank's market rate Northwind Bank on four statements, scored 1 to 5, then rate two rival banks on the same four. In Q3, "Fees are fair" fell to 3.2 from 3.9 while both rivals held steady, and the drop reached the brand lead in Slack.
fields.tab_content_2:
Old bag or new bag, never both

Before the new bag ships, 300 dog owners each see one design only and pick the words that fit from a list of eight. Of the 150 who saw the redesign, 95 picked premium, against 61 for the current bag. Natural slid to 66 from 87, and the design team put the green leaf back on the front.
fields.tab_content_3:
What one word says before the ratings start

Ahead of any rating question, small business owners type the first word that Ledgerline, a payroll app, brings to mind. Theme rules count pricey and costly as one. This month, 148 of 520 answers landed in that theme, and the tally posts to the brand research channel every Monday.
fields.tab_content_4:
Candidates rate the employer, hired or not

Two days after a final interview, every candidate gets a text asking whether they would tell a friend to apply. Each answer is saved with the role and panel. Last quarter, the 118 people turned down averaged 3.1 against 4.6 for the 62 hires, and the recruiting lead rewrote the rejection email first.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a Brand Perception Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to run a brand perception survey you can repeat each quarter and compare against rivals, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Rate competitors on the same scale
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick the group whose view you need, such as buyers in your category or customers who lapsed. Write one screening question for it, like a purchase in the past 12 months, and close the survey politely for anyone who does not qualify.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Before any brand name appears, ask what people think of when they hear your brand. Anyone shown a list first tends to pick from it instead of recalling, and the open answers lose their value. Keep this question on its own screen.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Draw the attributes from your positioning and from what buyers weigh when they choose, such as fair pricing or quick support. Phrase each one as a plain statement a person can agree with, and keep to one idea per line.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Repeat each statement for two or three competitors the respondent knows, in random order. A score of 3.8 means little alone. Next to a rival's 4.3, it tells you where you lose ground and by how much.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Lock the wording and the timing
fields.howto_step_5_des: Keep the statements, the scale, and the sample size fixed, and field each wave in the same weeks of the quarter. A changed word or a holiday month can move a score more than anything the brand did between waves.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Split each score by customer and non-customer, then by region or age band where the sample allows. Treat any segment with fewer than 50 answers as directional, and label it that way on the chart you share.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Act on the widest gap, then ask again
fields.howto_step_7_des: Pick the statement with the biggest gap to the leading rival and change one thing behind it, like fee wording or support hours. Run the next wave unchanged and check whether that gap narrowed for the people it was meant to reach.

plan.angle: The top 10 (Qualtrics, Attest, Hanover, Delighted, SurveyMonkey, QuestionPro, Typeform) are explainers and question lists: what perception is, 15 to 30 sample questions, a template. None shows what a perception survey looks like once it runs: the same statements asked wave after wave, rivals rated on the same scale, an unaided word question coded into themes, and a drop reaching someone who owns it. This page answers the question-bank intent in the FAQ and how-to, then shows four perception studies running: a quarterly attribute tracker against two rival banks, a split test of a redesigned pack, a first-word association question grouped by theme rules, and an employer brand survey sent to candidates after a final interview. The brand-awareness sibling owns recall and recognition; this page owns how people rate and describe a brand they already know.

claims_to_source: A brand perception survey measures how people view a brand, and is best run regularly and tracked over time
Unaided questions should be asked before aided questions or brand lists, because showing names first inflates the unaided answers
In a monadic test each respondent sees only one version of a concept, which limits order and comparison bias
Brand perception surveys ask respondents to rate a brand and each competitor on the same attribute statements and agreement scale, shown only for brands the respondent knows
Brand tracking repeats the same questions with a consistent sample at regular intervals, and changing wording between waves breaks the trend

scope.evidence: H1 "Build a Brand Perception Survey You Can Track Over Time", meta title "Brand Perception Survey Questions and Template | Emergent" and hero "Build a brand perception survey that rates you against rivals each quarter and keeps every answer in a database you own." cover the whole job; how-to description one sentence under 140 chars.

intent.evidence: Question-bank intent met in FAQ 4 ("the first word that comes to mind, agreement with attribute statements, and a comparison with named rivals"), template in FAQ 7, examples in FAQ 8, and a 7-step how-to.

specificity.evidence: Buyer vocabulary and real numbers: "\"Fees are fair\" fell to 3.2 from 3.9 while both rivals held steady"; "A score of 3.8 means little alone. Next to a rival's 4.3, it tells you where you lose ground".

openers.evidence: Feature bodies open on full sentences ("Rate the brand on four to six statements", "Ask the same statements", "Set the drop that matters"); tabs open on what happens ("Each quarter, 400 adults...").

craft.evidence: One idea per sentence: "Each statement you add costs three more ratings. Keep only those a decision depends on." Craft items recorded as notes.

voice.evidence: Reads operator-written: "Old bag or new bag, never both"; "the recruiting lead rewrote the rejection email first".

truth.evidence: meta_description: "four studies that rate your brand against rivals each quarter and flag any drop" is true of tab 1 only; tabs 2-4 contradict it.

distinct.evidence: Owns how people rate a brand they know (attribute statements, rival scores, word themes); awareness topics stay on the sibling. Cross-page formula reuse is a note.

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic questions, no brand or file-format asks, hub link in item 2, sibling links in items 4 and 8; FAQ 6 answers first: "Yes. Pick the two or three that buyers weigh against you".

images.evidence: Each tab matches its copy: "Fees are fair 3.9 3.2 -0.7", "Premium 61/95, Natural 87/66", "Pricey theme: 148 of 520" (212+148+96+64=520), "Hired 4.6 / Turned down 3.1, 118 answers"; one hero each, text readable.

findings.quote: four studies that rate your brand against rivals each quarter and flag any drop
findings.issue: The search snippet says all four studies rate the brand against rivals every quarter and flag drops. Only tab 1 (Northwind Bank) does. Tab 2 is a one-off pack test comparing the current bag with the redesign, with no rivals ("Before the new bag ships, 300 dog owners each see one design only"). Tab 3 counts first-word themes monthly for Ledgerline, with no rivals ("This month, 148 of 520 answers landed in that theme"). Tab 4 compares hires with turned-down candidates, with no rivals and no alert ("the 118 people turned down averaged 3.1 against 4.6 for the 62 hires"). No other field repeats the claim (hero, hero_prompt and H1 describe the survey you build, which is accurate).
findings.fix: Describe what the page actually shows, 110-160 chars, e.g. "Brand perception survey questions, a template, and four studies: a quarterly rival tracker, a pack redesign test, word themes, and candidate ratings."

findings.quote: A wave of 400 split across four regions leaves about 100 per region, thin for a score you mean to act on.
findings.issue: Two thresholds for a thin segment: FAQ 10 calls 100 answers thin, while howto_step_6_des says "Treat any segment with fewer than 50 answers as directional" and feature_4 says "segments under 50 answers are marked thin". A reader is left unsure whether 50 to 100 answers is enough to act on.
findings.fix: Align the advice: either keep 50 as the line everywhere or explain that 50 is the floor for showing a segment and 100 the floor for acting on it.

findings.quote: Sales figures show what people buy.
findings.issue: Answers that do not lead with the answer: FAQ 3 opens on sales figures and answers the purpose question in sentence 2; FAQ 5 ("Count the attribute statements first, since each one repeats for every rival.") gives a method but no number until the worked example.
findings.fix: Lead FAQ 3 with what the survey is for; lead FAQ 5 with a count, e.g. "About 15 to 20 ratings, plus a screener and the open question."
